summary: Trametinib (MEKINIST) is an oral reversible inhibitor of MEK1 and MEK2 kinases in the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK pathway. It is used to treat BRAF V600E/V600K-mutation-positive unresectable or metastatic melanoma (alone or with dabrafenib), BRAF V600E metastatic NSCLC and BRAF V600E anaplastic thyroid cancer (with dabrafenib), and adjuvant or other BRAF V600E solid tumors per the label. BRAF V600 mutation must be confirmed with an FDA-approved test; it is not effective and should not be used in wild-type BRAF tumors. The standard dose is 2 mg once daily on an empty stomach. Major risks include cardiomyopathy with decreased LVEF, ocular toxicity (retinal pigment epithelial detachment and retinal vein occlusion), serious skin toxicity/rash, interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, hemorrhage, venous thromboembolism, serious febrile reactions (especially in combination with dabrafenib), hyperglycemia, and embryo-fetal toxicity.
indications: BRAF V600E or V600K mutation-positive unresectable or metastatic melanoma, as a single agent or in combination with dabrafenib
Adjuvant treatment of BRAF V600E or V600K mutation-positive melanoma with involvement of lymph node(s) following complete resection, in combination with dabrafenib
BRAF V600E mutation-positive metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), in combination with dabrafenib
BRAF V600E mutation-positive locally advanced or metastatic anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC) with no satisfactory locoregional treatment options, in combination with dabrafenib

Adult and pediatric patients 6 years and older with unresectable or metastatic BRAF V600E mutation-positive solid tumors that have progressed following prior treatment and have no satisfactory alternatives, in combination with dabrafenib (limitation: not for colorectal cancer due to known intrinsic resistance)

admin: Take 2 mg orally once daily at the same time each day, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal
When combined with dabrafenib, take the trametinib dose with the morning dose or the evening dose of dabrafenib at the same time each day
Swallow tablets whole with water; do not crush
Assess LVEF by echocardiogram or MUGA at baseline, at 1 month, then every 2 to 3 months during treatment
Obtain an ophthalmologic evaluation for any visual disturbances and at periodic intervals as clinically indicated
Do not initiate in patients with a wild-type BRAF tumor; confirm BRAF V600E/V600K with an FDA-approved test before starting
moa: Trametinib is a reversible, allosteric inhibitor of mitogen-activated extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1 (MEK1) and MEK2 activation and kinase activity. MEK1 and MEK2 are central components of the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK signaling pathway, which promotes cell proliferation. BRAF V600 mutations cause constitutive activation of this pathway. By inhibiting MEK1/MEK2, trametinib blocks downstream ERK phosphorylation and tumor cell growth driven by activated BRAF. Trametinib and dabrafenib (a BRAF inhibitor) target two different kinases in the same pathway; the combination produces greater inhibition of pathway signaling and antitumor activity than either agent alone in BRAF V600-mutated tumors, and may delay the emergence of resistance.

absolute: No contraindications are listed in the product label (None)
relative: Wild-type BRAF tumor (not indicated and not effective)
Baseline LVEF below institutional lower limit of normal or significant cardiac dysfunction
History of retinal vein occlusion or other significant ocular disease
monitor: Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) at baseline, 1 month, then every 2-3 months
Ophthalmologic evaluation for visual symptoms (RPED, retinal vein occlusion)
Skin for serious rash and skin toxicity
Pulmonary symptoms for interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis
Signs of bleeding and venous thromboembolism
Body temperature for serious febrile reactions (especially with dabrafenib) and serum glucose

preg: Based on its mechanism of action and animal data, trametinib can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman. Animal studies showed teratogenicity and embryofetal lethality at exposures below the human exposure at the recommended dose. Advise pregnant women of the potential risk to a fetus. Females of reproductive potential should use effective contraception during treatment and for 4 months after the last dose. When used with dabrafenib, dabrafenib can render hormonal contraceptives ineffective, so an alternative non-hormonal method is recommended.
lact: There are no data on the presence of trametinib in human milk or its effects on the breastfed child or on milk production. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a breastfed child, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment with trametinib and for 4 months after the last dose.
renal: No dosage adjustment is recommended for patients with mild or moderate renal impairment based on population pharmacokinetic analysis. The pharmacokinetics of trametinib have not been studied in patients with severe renal impairment; use with caution as no specific guidance is available.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment is recommended for patients with mild hepatic impairment based on population pharmacokinetic analysis. The appropriate dose has not been established for patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment; use with caution and monitor closely.

major: Anticoagulants/antiplatelet agents - additive risk of hemorrhage, including major and fatal intracranial or GI bleeding; weigh benefit and monitor closely
moderate: Other agents that prolong QT or affect cardiac function - additive cardiotoxicity risk; monitor LVEF
Hyperglycemia-inducing drugs (e.g., corticosteroids) - may worsen drug-induced hyperglycemia; monitor glucose
Dabrafenib (intended combination) - dabrafenib is a CYP3A/CYP2C inducer that can reduce levels of co-administered drugs and render hormonal contraceptives ineffective
minor: No clinically significant minor interactions are documented; trametinib has low potential for CYP-mediated drug interactions
interactions.food: Administer at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal; a high-fat, high-calorie meal decreases trametinib AUC and Cmax, so take on an empty stomach.
interactions.alcohol: No specific alcohol interaction is described in the label.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor LVEF (echocardiogram/MUGA), serum glucose, and obtain ophthalmologic examinations; confirm BRAF V600 mutation by an FDA-approved test.

serious: Cardiomyopathy with decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF)
Ocular toxicity (retinal pigment epithelial detachment [RPED], retinal vein occlusion [RVO])
Serious skin toxicity and severe rash
Hemorrhage (including fatal intracranial and GI bleeding)
Serious febrile reactions/pyrexia (especially in combination with dabrafenib)
rare: New primary malignancies (cutaneous and non-cutaneous, mainly when used with dabrafenib)
emergency: Acute heart failure from cardiomyopathy/decreased LVEF
Sudden vision loss (retinal vein occlusion or RPED)
Pulmonary embolism or other venous thromboembolism
Acute interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis with respiratory distress
Severe febrile reaction with hypotension, dehydration, or renal failure

monitoring: LVEF by echocardiogram or MUGA at baseline, at 1 month, then every 2 to 3 months
Ophthalmologic evaluation for any visual disturbances (RPED, retinal vein occlusion)
Skin examinations for serious rash/skin toxicity and new primary skin cancers
Pulmonary symptoms (dyspnea, cough, hypoxia) for interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis
Signs of bleeding and venous thromboembolism; body temperature for serious febrile reactions
Serum glucose (especially in patients with diabetes or hyperglycemia)
counsel: Take one 2 mg tablet once daily at the same time each day, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal
Report any shortness of breath, swelling of the legs, or signs of heart problems, and report chest pain or palpitations
Report changes in vision such as blurred vision, loss of vision, or other visual changes right away
Report new or worsening skin rash, fever, cough or breathing problems, unusual bleeding, or leg swelling/pain
Avoid pregnancy; use effective contraception during and for 4 months after treatment, and do not breastfeed; tell your doctor about all medicines
pk: Antitumor pathway inhibition with steady-state reached in about 15 days of once-daily dosing
Median time to peak concentration about 1.5 hours after oral dosing; bioavailability ~72%
Long half-life supports once-daily dosing; pathway inhibition sustained over the dosing interval
Store refrigerated at 2-8 C (36-46 F); protect from light and moisture
pearls: Confirm a BRAF V600E/V600K mutation with an FDA-approved test before starting; not effective in wild-type BRAF tumors
Assess LVEF at baseline, 1 month, then every 2-3 months; cardiomyopathy/decreased LVEF can be reversible with dose interruption/reduction
Get an ophthalmologic evaluation for visual symptoms - retinal pigment epithelial detachment is often reversible, but permanently discontinue for retinal vein occlusion
Combination with dabrafenib increases serious febrile reactions (pyrexia) - manage with dose interruption and antipyretics; also watch for new primary malignancies
Take on an empty stomach (1 hour before or 2 hours after food); store tablets in the refrigerator
missed: If a dose is missed, it can be taken as soon as remembered. However, do not take a missed dose if it is less than 12 hours before the next scheduled dose; instead skip the missed dose and take the next dose at the regular time. Do not take an extra dose to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: There is no specific antidote for trametinib overdose. In the event of overdose, treatment should consist of general supportive measures with monitoring for adverse reactions, including cardiac (LVEF), ocular, dermatologic, and hematologic toxicity. Because trametinib is highly protein bound, dialysis is unlikely to be effective in significantly enhancing its elimination.
